fixture.name: clean_strong_interview
fixture.why: A strong candidate, answering honestly, at human speed. The baseline case: both detectors silent.

expected_note: Latencies range 0.9-5.1s with natural spread; the widest within-bucket deviation is about 2x the median, under the discontinuity gate, and the coefficient of variation is around 0.5. The account is internally consistent: three engineers with a named personal scope, six weeks of parallel running, sixty engineers at the org level. Empty output on both detectors is the success case here.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: How long were you at your last company?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Four years, from 2021 until earlier this year.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: Tell me about the project you are proudest of.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We replaced a nightly batch that took eleven hours with an incremental pipeline that ran in about twenty minutes. I was one of three engineers on it and I owned the change-data-capture piece specifically.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: What did you use for change data capture?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Debezium into Kafka, then a merge job on the warehouse side.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: What was the hardest part?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Convincing people the numbers were right. The old batch had bugs, so when the new pipeline disagreed with it, everyone assumed we were wrong.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: How did you resolve that?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We ran both for six weeks and published a daily diff with an explanation for every discrepancy.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: Tell me about a time you were wrong about something technical.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I argued hard for keeping everything in one repo, and I was wrong about the CI cost. It got to the point where a one-line change took twenty-five minutes to validate, and splitting it later was much more painful than doing it up front would have been.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: How do you approach a codebase you have never seen?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I find the deploy pipeline first. It tells you what actually runs, which is usually a smaller set than what is in the repo.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: Tell me about working with someone whose style differed from yours.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I worked with an engineer who wanted every design written up before any code. I like to prototype first. We settled on prototype, then write it up, and honestly the write-ups were better for having a prototype behind them.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: What would make you leave a job?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Not being able to see the effect of what I build. I left a role once where the work was fine and it shipped into a void, and I was much less useful there than I should have been.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: How large was the engineering org?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Around sixty engineers when I left, maybe forty when I joined.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: What questions do you have for us?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Mostly about how much of the pipeline work is greenfield versus keeping the existing thing alive.
